note.text: Track hypotheses as (nexiom pair, response rule), not pairs alone. Non-nexioms never matter; a negative test does not exclude any individual object. Here the true pair was kurife and paralil. Every test contained exactly one of them, so four negatives were consistent with an AND rule. My answer, fekara and degakon, was only another compatible guess—not a deduction. Testing all objects could distinguish AND from exactly-one behavior, provided those are the candidate rules. Before each test, partition surviving hypotheses by predicted outcome and choose an informative split. Check whether identification is actually guaranteed within the remaining budget; four binary results offer only 16 outcome paths for 15 pairs, leaving almost no room for unknown-rule ambiguity. Predict singleton probes from surviving rules rather than from an unverified guessed pair.

note.text: Track hypotheses as (nexiom pair, response rule), not pairs alone. This time my answer, tadopes and sutugos, was correct. However, every negative test contained tadopes without sutugos, and every positive test contained both. Thus I learned that tadopes alone does not activate the machine and that both together do. I did NOT learn what sutugos alone does: both an AND rule and a sutugos-controlled rule fit these observations. My “PROBE: no” was therefore an unsupported guess. For future machines, retain all response rules consistent with the evidence, including asymmetric rules. Choose tests that divide the surviving hypotheses, and distinguish identifying the pair from identifying the rule. Before predicting an untested configuration, check whether every surviving hypothesis predicts the same outcome. Four binary tests leave little room to identify both an unknown pair and an unknown rule reliably.
